title: Researchers disagree on whether a longer look means the baby keeps the hidden object in mind
summary: One opened paper reads longer looking at an impossible hiding as an expectation about a hidden object, and another says a longer look can be a path expectation without permanence.
body: Two opened papers disagree about what a longer look at an 'impossible' hiding shows, and they do not report the same display. This card keeps both readings and does not choose one. Wang and colleagues measured a wide object behind a narrow screen. Meltzoff and Moore discuss a tall rabbit that fails to appear in a gap, and they say looking time alone cannot separate a path expectation from permanence.

sources.title: Young infants' reasoning about hidden objects: evidence from violation-of-expectation tasks with test trials only
sources.author: Su-hua Wang, Renée Baillargeon, and Laura Brueckner
sources.note: One side: the authors' reading that longer looking indexed an expectation about a hidden object.

sources.title: Object representation, identity, and the paradox of early permanence
sources.author: Andrew N. Meltzoff and M. Keith Moore
sources.note: Other side: longer looking at the tall-rabbit event can follow from trajectory extrapolation without permanence, and looking time does not separate the two.

said_by: Wang, Baillargeon, and Brueckner; Meltzoff and Moore

contested_views.label: Longer looking shows a hidden-object expectation
contested_views.summary: Wang, Baillargeon, and Brueckner read longer looking when a wide object vanished behind a too-narrow screen as evidence the infants represented the hidden object.

sources.title: Young infants' reasoning about hidden objects: evidence from violation-of-expectation tasks with test trials only
sources.author: Su-hua Wang, Renée Baillargeon, and Laura Brueckner

contested_views.label: Longer looking can be a path expectation
contested_views.summary: Meltzoff and Moore argue that longer looking when a tall rabbit fails to appear in a gap can come from expecting the object along its path, without permanence, and that looking time does not separate the readings.

sources.title: Object representation, identity, and the paradox of early permanence
sources.author: Andrew N. Meltzoff and M. Keith Moore
sources.note: Their alternative to Baillargeon's tall-and-short rabbit reading. Infant Behavior and Development 1998;21(2):201-235.
